 --> Vasu Baras 2026: Govatsa Dwadashi date, puja muhurat, rituals, fasting rules and significance of the Diwali festival
 Vasu Baras 2026 falls on November 5. Know the Govatsa Dwadashi puja muhurat, vrat katha, rituals, fasting rules and significance of the festival marking Diwali's beginning in Maharashtra. 
 MC Religion Desk 
 November 05, 2026 / 12:20 IST Share --> 
 --> 
 -->

 Vasu Baras 2026: Govatsa Dwadashi date, puja muhurat, rituals, fasting rules and significance of the Diwali festival (image: canva) Vasu Baras 2026 falls on Thursday, November 5.
 It marks the start of Diwali in Maharashtra.
 Devotees worship cows and calves for prosperity.

 Vasu Baras, also known as Govatsa Dwadashi, will be celebrated on Thursday, November 5, 2026, marking the beginning of Diwali festivities in Maharashtra. Dedicated to the worship of cows and their calves, the festival holds deep religious and cultural significance in Hindu tradition. It is observed with prayers, fasting and rituals that express gratitude for the role of cows in providing nourishment and supporting agricultural life. 
 The festival is associated with prosperity, motherhood, abundance and family well-being. Devotees, particularly married women and mothers, observe the day to seek blessings for the health, happiness and longevity of their children. Vasu Baras is also celebrated in Gujarat, where it is known as Vagh Baras. 
 Govatsa Dwadashi falls on the Dwadashi Tithi, the 12th lunar day of Krishna Paksha, or the waning phase of the moon. In Maharashtra, it is regarded as the first day of the Diwali celebrations, preceding Dhanteras. 
 Vasu Baras 2026 date and puja muhurat 
 According to Drik Panchang, Vasu Baras will be observed on November 5, 2026. The festival's puja is traditionally performed during the evening Pradosh period, which is considered auspicious for worshipping cows and calves.  Here are the key timings for Govatsa Dwadashi 2026: 
 Vasu Baras date: Thursday, November 5, 2026 
 Dwadashi Tithi begins: 10:35 am on November 5 
 Dwadashi Tithi ends: 10:30 am on November 6 
 Govatsa Dwadashi Puja Muhurat: 5:33 pm to 8:10 pm on November 5 
 The puja timings may vary from one location to another, depending on local Panchang calculations. Devotees are advised to check the timings for their respective cities before performing the rituals. 
 Vasu Baras is observed a day before Dhanteras and is considered the opening day of Diwali festivities in Maharashtra. The celebrations are followed by Dhanteras, Narak Chaturdashi, Lakshmi Puja, Bali Pratipada and Bhai Dooj, though the sequence may differ according to regional calendars. 
 Vasu Baras significance: Why are Cows worshipped? 
 Govatsa Dwadashi carries religious, cultural and spiritual importance in Hinduism. Cows are considered sacred and are associated with Kamadhenu, the divine wish-fulfilling cow. Worshipping a cow and her calf on this day is seen as an expression of gratitude for their contribution to nourishment, farming and everyday life. 
 The festival also has a special significance for mothers. Married women, particularly those with children, observe the Vasu Baras vrat to pray for their children's health, longevity, happiness and prosperity. According to religious beliefs, sincere observance of the fast and rituals is believed to bring blessings to the family. 
 The name 'Vasu Baras' has a traditional association with prosperity and wealth. 'Baras' refers to the twelfth lunar day, while 'Vasu' is linked with abundance and good fortune. The observance is therefore regarded as a way of seeking prosperity, spiritual merit and well-being.  
 In Maharashtra, Vasu Baras is an important part of the Diwali calendar, bringing together devotion, family traditions and reverence for cattle. 
 Vasu Baras puja vidhi: Rituals to observe on Govatsa Dwadashi 
 The central ritual of Vasu Baras is the worship of a cow and her calf. Devotees follow customary practices that may vary between households and regions. The commonly observed puja vidhi includes the following steps: 
 1. Wake up early and take a bath 
 Devotees begin the day with an early morning bath. The house and the area designated for the puja are cleaned and prepared for the rituals. 
 2. Clean and decorate the Cow and Calf 
 The cow and her calf are cleaned and decorated with flowers and garlands. Turmeric, kumkum or sandalwood paste may be applied to their foreheads as part of the traditional worship. 
 3. Perform Govatsa Dwadashi puja 
 Devotees offer flowers, incense, a diya, akshata (rice grains) and other puja materials. Water may also be offered at the feet of the cow. Prayers are recited to seek blessings for the family's well-being and prosperity. 
 4. Offer food to the Cow and Calf 
 Special food offerings are prepared and given to the cow and calf. Depending on local customs, these may include wheat-based preparations, jaggery, gram or other suitable fodder. 
 5. Perform Aarti 
 Aarti is performed in front of the cow and calf. Devotees pray for the health, happiness and prosperity of their children and family members. 
 6. Listen to the Govatsa Dwadashi vrat katha 
 The traditional Vrat Katha associated with Govatsa Dwadashi is recited or heard during the puja. The story is considered an important part of the religious observance. 
 7. Observe the vrat 
 Devotees, especially women observing the fast, follow their family's prescribed fasting customs. The fast is concluded according to the rituals followed in the household. 
 Vasu Baras 2026: Fasting rules and food customs 
 Fasting is an important aspect of Vasu Baras for many devotees. However, the rules differ according to regional practices and family traditions.  Some commonly followed customs include: 
 Avoiding wheat-based food during the fast. 
 Refraining from consuming cow's milk and milk-based products, such as curd, ghee and buttermilk, in traditions that prescribe this restriction. 
 Observing a full-day fast or consuming permitted foods, depending on household customs. 
 Offering food to the cow and calf before eating. 
 Consuming a simple and satvik meal after the puja. 
 In some Maharashtra households, wheat and moong dal are avoided on Govatsa Dwadashi. These restrictions are not universal, and devotees generally follow the fasting rules prescribed by their family or regional tradition. 
 Govatsa Dwadashi vrat katha: The story of divine Cow Nandini 
 Govatsa Dwadashi is closely associated with Nandini, the divine cow believed in Hindu mythology to be the daughter of Kamadhenu. Nandini is said to possess the power to fulfil the wishes of devotees and is also associated with sage Vashistha.  Because of this connection, the festival is sometimes referred to as Nandini Vrat. The worship of cows and calves is linked with the blessings, nourishment and prosperity believed to be associated with the divine cow. 
 Different regional traditions narrate distinct stories about Govatsa Dwadashi. Some versions recount the story of a woman who observes a fast after being separated from her child, while others focus on Nandini and the blessings received through devotion to cows.  The vrat katha forms an important part of the observance, reinforcing the festival's themes of maternal love, devotion, gratitude and family well-being. 
 Vasu Baras: The beginning of Diwali celebrations in Maharashtra 
 Vasu Baras is more than a religious observance. It reflects the longstanding cultural connection between cattle, agriculture and household prosperity. The worship of cows and calves highlights their traditional role in sustaining rural life and providing nourishment. 
 As the first day of Diwali festivities in Maharashtra, Govatsa Dwadashi sets the tone for the celebrations that follow. Through prayers, fasting and the worship of cattle, devotees seek blessings for a prosperous and healthy year ahead.
